scenes.text: Luna climbed a little hill with a lantern in her hand. Two travelers were sitting among the flowers. “Hello! Are you watching the stars, too?” she asked.
“Yes! Come and sit with us,” said Leo. Noah moved a little to make room. The three friends looked up at the sky. A small group of stars caught Luna’s eye.
“What are those stars called?” Luna asked. “They’re called the Seven Sisters,” Leo replied. Noah smiled. “That’s interesting. In New Zealand, I learned a different name for them.”
“Where did you learn that name?” asked Luna. “In Greece,” said Leo. “But what about you?” Luna remembered the nights she spent with her grandmother in Japan.
“In Japan, this group of stars is called Subaru,” Luna explained. “The name is said to come from an old word about things coming together, just like these little stars.”
“When did people start using that name?” asked Noah. “A very long time ago! Subaru is mentioned in a Japanese book called The Pillow Book. It was written by Sei Shōnagon.”
Luna remembered sitting beside her grandmother on a cold night. “How many stars can you see?” her grandmother asked. Luna counted them slowly. “One, two, three… I can see six!”
“There are many more stars in that group,” Luna told her friends. “Some are hard to see with our eyes, but more can be seen through a telescope.”
Leo opened his book. “In an old Greek myth, the stars are known as the Seven Sisters. They were the daughters of Atlas and Pleione. Would you like to hear their story?”
“Long ago, seven sisters lived together,” Leo began. “One day, they were chased by a hunter named Orion. They ran as fast as they could, but they couldn’t get away.”
“Oh no! How did they become stars?” Luna asked. “In one version of the story, they were placed in the sky by Zeus, who wanted to keep them safe,” said Leo.
“And now, the sisters shine together,” Leo said, closing his book. Luna looked at the little stars again. “I like that story. I’m glad the sisters are safe.”
“Where I grew up, many people call this group Matariki,” said Noah. “For many Māori communities, these stars mark the beginning of the Māori New Year.”
“When is Matariki celebrated?” asked Luna. “In the middle of winter,” Noah replied. “The stars appear again in the sky just before sunrise. Some communities mark the new year with other stars.”
“Is there a story about these stars, too?” asked Leo. “Yes. In one Māori story, Matariki is a mother surrounded by six daughters. Each daughter has a special gift.”
“How do they use their gifts?” Luna asked. “They visit their great-grandmother, Papatūānuku, the Earth,” said Noah. “They help care for the plants and the natural world as a new year approaches.”

“How is the new year celebrated?” asked Leo. “Families and friends come together,” Noah explained. “People who have died are remembered. Food is shared, and people talk about their hopes for the future.”
Luna opened her notebook. “Subaru, the Seven Sisters, and Matariki,” she said. “Three different names for the same group of stars.” Leo smiled. “And so many stories to discover!”
“Where will you go next?” Noah asked. “I’ll travel to another town,” said Luna. “I want to hear more stories.” Leo nodded. “And I’ll tell people about the stories we heard tonight.”
Before they left, the three friends looked up one last time. “We come from different places,” said Luna, “and we tell different stories. But we all look up at the same sky.”
